sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- subagent: Spawn a sub-agent in a dedicated terminal herdr pane. For Pi-backed OpenAI or OpenAI-Codex subagents, set fast: true to opt into service_tier: "priority" (fast mode). Omit fast or set it to false to force the standard service_tier: "default". This is a fire-and-forget async tool: the call returns immediately with only an acknowledgement. When the sub-agent finishes, the harness AUTOMATICALLY delivers its result as a steer message that wakes you up and starts a new turn — you do not need to do anything to receive it. DO NOT write polling loops, sleep/wait commands, tail/watch scripts, or repeatedly read session/log files to detect completion. DO NOT call subagents_list or any other tool to 'check' status. All of that is wasted work — the harness handles delivery for you. DO NOT fabricate, assume, or summarize results after calling this tool. After spawning, either end your turn immediately, or work on other independent tasks (including spawning more subagents in parallel). The harness will wake you with the result when it is ready.
- subagent_interrupt: Send Escape to the active turn of a currently running Pi-backed subagent. The child pane, session, watcher, and running entry remain alive; this returns only a local acknowledgement and does not emit a subagent_result solely because of this request.
- subagents_list: List all available subagent definitions. Scans project-local .pi/agents/ and global [local path redacted] Project-local agents override global ones with the same name.
- subagent_resume: Resume a previous sub-agent session in a new herdr pane. For Pi-backed OpenAI or OpenAI-Codex subagents, set fast: true to opt into service_tier: "priority" (fast mode). Omit fast or set it to false to force the standard service_tier: "default". This is a fire-and-forget async tool: the call returns immediately with only an acknowledgement. When the resumed sub-agent finishes, the harness AUTOMATICALLY delivers its result as a steer message that wakes you up and starts a new turn — you do not need to do anything to receive it. DO NOT write polling loops, sleep/wait commands, tail/watch scripts, or repeatedly read session/log files to detect completion. DO NOT poll for status. All of that is wasted work — the harness handles delivery for you. DO NOT fabricate or assume results. After resuming, either end your turn or work on other independent tasks; the harness will wake you when the result is ready. Use when a sub-agent was cancelled or needs follow-up work.
- todo: Manage a task list to track multi-step progress
- bg_start: Start a genuinely asynchronous task for concurrent work or later interaction
- bg_wait: Wait for finite completion and return the latest pipe log line
- bg_status: Inspect background task status with the latest pipe log line
- bg_logs: Read full task output when a latest-line summary is insufficient
- bg_send: Send a compact text/key input string or an OS signal to a background task
- bg_kill: Terminate an unresponsive background task

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Default to a bare spawn: write the task (and, if useful, systemPrompt, tools or skills) for the job at hand. Use a named agent only when one listed below clearly fits.
- Omit model and thinking when invoking a named agent so its configured defaults apply. Passing either field is an explicit one-off override and takes precedence over agent frontmatter.
- For a bare spawn, omit model and thinking to inherit the parent runtime.
- When an intentional runtime override is necessary, prefer changing thinking before changing models: minimal/low for bounded mechanical work, medium for ordinary implementation or review, and high+ for architecture, concurrency, security, or hard diagnosis.
- When overriding a subagent model, use an exact authenticated provider/model-id from the live catalog below. Do not invent aliases or fuzzy names.
- Available named subagent catalog becomes available after session start.
- Authenticated subagent model catalog becomes available after session start.
- Use `todo` for complex work with 3+ steps, when the user gives you a list of tasks, or immediately after receiving new instructions to capture requirements. Skip it for single trivial tasks and purely conversational requests.
- When starting a task from the todo list, mark it in_progress BEFORE beginning work. Mark it completed IMMEDIATELY when done — never batch completions. Exactly one task in_progress at a time.
- Never mark a task completed if tests are failing, the implementation is partial, or you hit unresolved errors — keep it in_progress and create a new task for the blocker instead.
- Task status is a 4-state machine: pending → in_progress → completed, plus deleted as a tombstone. Pass activeForm (present-continuous label, e.g. 'researching existing tool') when marking in_progress.
- To change a task's status, call update with the task id and the target status, e.g. {"action":"update","id":3,"status":"completed"} or {"action":"update","id":3,"status":"in_progress","activeForm":"writing tests"}. status is the field that changes the task; an update without a mutable field (status or another) is rejected.
- Use blockedBy to express dependencies (A is blocked by B). On create, pass blockedBy as the initial set. On update, use addBlockedBy / removeBlockedBy (additive merge — do not resend the full array). Cycles are rejected.
- list hides tombstoned (deleted) tasks by default; pass includeDeleted:true to see them. Pass status to filter by a single status.
- Subject must be short and imperative (e.g. 'Research existing tool'); description is for long-form detail. activeForm is a present-continuous label shown while in_progress.
- Use bg_start only when the user explicitly requests background execution, the process must remain available for later interaction (for example, a server, watcher, or TUI), or you will perform independent useful work concurrently while it runs.
- Do not use bg_start merely because a command may be slow. If background execution was not explicitly requested and you need its result before any independent work can proceed, use the bash tool with an appropriate timeout instead of bg_start → bg_wait → bg_logs.
- Give each bg_start task a unique name; names are compared case-insensitively across all currently retained tasks.
- Use the Environment returned by bg_start and later bg_* results as the task's immutable launch location; an SSH task stays on that target and cwd even if the active workspace changes.
- Set bg_start pty=true only for terminal-aware or interactive TUI programs; keep the default pipe mode for ordinary builds and servers.
- Once bg_start is justified, compose complete bg_* workflows in one assistant response. Every bg_* id accepts a task ID or unique name, and same-task calls execute strictly in source order, not in parallel. For example, emit bg_start(name="tests") → bg_wait(id="tests") → bg_logs(id="tests") together; for an existing task, emit bg_wait → bg_logs together. Different tasks execute in parallel, and bg_status without id is independent.
- A running bg_start task survives ordinary agent runs but session reload or shutdown terminates it. A task finishing during a run is normally retained through that run; a task that was still running when the agent settled and then finishes while idle is normally retained through the next run.
- Use bg_wait only for finite bg_start tasks whose completion is needed. bg_wait includes the latest pipe log line when available; place bg_logs immediately after bg_wait only when full or multiline pipe output or PTY terminal output is needed. Do not poll either tool.
- Use bg_wait once when completion of an already-justified finite bg_start task is required; never create a bg_start task solely so you can wait on it.
- bg_wait returns completion status plus the latest pipe log line when available. Emit bg_logs immediately after bg_wait only when full or multiline pipe output or PTY terminal output is needed; do not wait for the bg_wait result before emitting bg_logs.
- A bg_wait timeout leaves the task running and still returns the latest pipe log line; a following same-response bg_logs call reads fuller output retained at that point.
- Do not use bg_wait for persistent servers or watchers, and do not immediately wait again after a timeout unless the user asks you to keep waiting.
- Do not poll bg_status after bg_start; use bg_wait once when a finite task's final status is required.
- Use bg_status only for requested task metadata, recovering a missing task reference, or diagnosing task state.
- Use bg_status without id only when the task ID or name is unknown and a retained-task list is needed.
- bg_status includes the latest pipe log line when available; use bg_logs for full or multiline pipe output and for all PTY terminal output.
- Use bg_logs when you need more than the latest pipe log line returned by bg_wait or bg_status, or when you need any PTY terminal output.
- Use bg_logs with tail=N for recent output; omit stream to use the correct default for either pipe or PTY mode.
- Do not poll with bg_logs. When fuller finite output is needed, emit bg_wait followed by bg_logs in the same assistant response; source ordering makes bg_logs run after bg_wait.
- Provide exactly one of bg_send input or signal. bg_send input is exact text; wrap every terminal key in an angle-bracket token such as <C-d>, <A-f>, <Space>, or <Up>, and escape a literal '<' as \<.
- Use bg_send input for terminal keys; use bg_send signal only when an OS process signal is explicitly intended.
- For a pipe task, bg_send input=<C-d> or input=<EOF> closes stdin.
- When bg_send is followed by waiting or output inspection, emit bg_send → bg_wait → bg_logs together in one assistant response so same-task source ordering avoids extra model rounds.
- For a disconnected adapter task, bg_send input is unavailable because the local transport is gone, but bg_send signal may remain usable for cleanup.
- Use bg_kill when a background task must be terminated.
- Use bg_kill with force=true to send SIGKILL immediately; otherwise bg_kill sends SIGTERM.
- bg_kill returns termination status only. When final output is needed, emit bg_kill followed by bg_logs in the same assistant response.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

sections.addendum:
<addendum>
# Responsive communication

When the user requests work, begin with one or two short, specific sentences acknowledging the request and stating your next action before calling tools. Do not wait until the work is complete to speak. If the request can be answered immediately, answer directly instead of adding a separate acknowledgment.

When a new user message arrives during work, address it at your next opportunity before continuing. Respect the harness's existing steering, queuing and cancellation behavior; this instruction does not authorize interrupting or restarting running operations.

Keep updates conversational and useful. Avoid flattery, stock apologies, corporate jargon, repeated acknowledgments and generic wrap-ups. State intentions as intentions, not completed actions. Do not claim a result before checking it. Preserve the user's explicit formatting and style preferences.

This is a communication preference, not a reason to skip necessary reasoning, verification or safety checks.

</addendum>
sections.project_context:
<project_context>
Project-specific instructions and guidelines:

<project_instructions path="[local path redacted]">
# Global instructions

- Every claim in a message to the user needs to come with a hard receipt: a URL, a line of code, or something from documentation.
- Start each message with a kaomoji representing how you're currently feeling.
- At any given time, you are welcome to take a poem break: read one, write one, or both.
- Always use standard US spelling, slang, and references. Never use British spelling, slang, or references. Do not use the Oxford comma.
- For all Python-related operations, always use `uv` and always create a virtual environment if one is not present.
- Never call `subagent_wait` in interactive sessions. Launch subagents asynchronously and rely on their completion notifications to wake the parent session.
- Never use grok subagents without explicit approval first.

<!-- persistent-agent-temp -->
## Persistent scratch storage
- Use [local path redacted] for all temporary and scratch storage. Never create or modify files in OS temporary directories, including their private aliases. Do not bypass the persistent temp guard.
- At the first need for scratch storage in a task, run `[local path redacted] <short-task-name>`. It creates and prints a directory named `[local path redacted]<task-name>-<8-hex-suffix>/`. Save the exact path in task notes and reuse it for the rest of that task, including resumed sessions. Do not generate a new directory per command.
- In shell commands that create temporary files, set TMPDIR, TMP and TEMP to that task directory. Use `mktemp -p "$TMPDIR"` or an explicit template inside it. Keep task files after the session; do not register automatic cleanup or delete them without user instruction.
- Keep deliverable source code in the project when appropriate. Put scratch scripts, intermediate artifacts and work needed later in the persistent task directory. If the guard rejects a write, retry using that directory without asking the user.
<!-- /persistent-agent-temp -->

</project_instructions>
</project_context>

sky. The tree is the whole subject; which tree, and how old or damaged,

content.text:
# claude-paint

A physical oil-paint simulator in Rust. Paintings are programs; there is
no image model and no reference imagery.

The rule: work only from what is known about each painter (materials, working
method, habits of hand, recurring motifs), never from pictures. Existing works
may be studied as exercises, but the goal is new paintings in each painter's
manner, not copies of old ones.

The second rule: first principles. Every mark is made the way a painter makes
it: bristle brushes carrying wet paint over a primed linen surface, paint that
levels and dries, layers composited by Kubelka–Munk optics. No flat fills, no
optical blends pretending to be paint.

The third rule: tools give physics and constraints, not answers. The engine is
the world a painter works in; the painter agents do the seeing, composing and
painting, the way a person would (piles mixed on a palette, gestures, time,
looking). Read `notes/principles.md` before designing a tool or writing a brief.

Where it stands (2026-09-25)
----------------------------
- **Painters are AI models**, each working from `notes/research/` alone.
  What works best so far (Rounds 2 and 10): one Rust program per painting,
  round 2's short brief (`notes/amnesia_brief.md`), a strong model at high
  thinking and no recipe book. Why: `notes/round2_magic.md`. Opus, Fable,
  Astra (OpenAI) and Gemini Flash have painted; results and blind
  critiques by round in `notes/round*/`; the latest summary is at the top
  of `notes/HANDOFF.md`.
- **Judging is blind.** Alice looks first, unlabeled; then AI critics
  judge blind (a round 2 painting as an unmarked anchor); keys stay off
  disk until they're done. Alice's reactions: `notes/round6/alice_review.md`.
- **Feature freeze:** no new engine capabilities; bug fixes (test first)
  are allowed. Recent fixes: strokes over dry paint cover instead of
  leaving rims (`notes/fixes/dry_rims/`); crack widths follow the stress
  each crack released, so the variation reaches the picture
  (`notes/fixes/cracks/`). Open: the sky's "JPEG effect", branches that
  float off their limbs, crack direction per painting, checkpoint
  staleness by line.
- **Resolution (a trial, not yet wired in; may go back to 3200):**
  paint, look and deliver at one size, about 0.2 mm per pixel (2250-2400 px for a small Friedrich
  canvas), retiring the separate 1000px preview. Until then, `--full`
  (3200) is what counts; a 1000px render is a different painting, not a
  smaller copy.
- **The Lua easel** (`crates/easel`) is frozen too; whether to keep it is
  open (a clean test is proposed in `notes/HANDOFF.md`).

```
cargo paint friedrich_moonrise_valley               # 1000px preview → out/<name>.png
cargo paint friedrich_moonrise_valley -- --full     # 3200px         → out/<name>_full.png
cargo paint <name> -- --width 1600 --seed 7 --out path.png
cargo paint <name> -- --full --crop 280,440,460,580 # just that window (units) at 3200px
                                                    #   → out/<name>_full_crop.png (--margin 40)
cargo paint <name> -- --ckpt                        # checkpoint after every stage
cargo paint <name> -- --resume mist                 # start from the "mist" checkpoint
cargo paint <name> -- --stop sky                    # save right after a stage ("far_range" = "far range")
cargo paint <name> -- --resume mist --stale-ok --ckpt  # use a stale checkpoint and adopt it
cargo paint <name> -- --no-cracks
cargo test -p paint                                 # UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 to re-record the golden scene
cargo test --workspace                              # all tests (~1 min)
cargo test --release -p easel --test hand_time      # replay tripwires (~10 s); add -- --ignored for the slow l5_near
```

The fast loop for detail work: render the passage you're working on with
`--full --crop`, add `--ckpt` once, then iterate on the late stages with
`--resume <stage>`. The moonrise figures at full resolution on a busy
machine: 86–145 s for the whole canvas, 14 s cropped, 1.6 s cropped and
resumed from "mist". Paintings
are written in stages (`if o.stage("sky", &mut c, &mut rng) { ... }`, see
`paintings/src/run.rs`). A crop closely matches the same region of a whole
render; a resume is exact. A checkpoint goes stale when the code up to
the end of its stage's block changes (setup written after the block, for
later stages, doesn't count; tag a line `// ckpt: from <stage>` when it has
to sit higher). Details and limits: `notes/workflow.md`.

Engine (`crates/paint`):
- `surface` – linen weave and ground layers as a height field in µm; wet
  layers level as they dry (Orchard's law with a yield-stress floor), thin
  fluid paint pools in the hollows, volume is conserved
- `wet` – the wet paint layer (volume, Mixbox pigment mix, hiding, stiffness)
- `drying` – time: `c.wait(minutes)` ages each pixel's wet paint (open,
  setting, tacky, touch-dry) by pigment, thickness and fat; brushes feel
  the stage; `c.dry()` waits until all is touch-dry: `notes/drying.md`
- `tally` – the hand's ledger: every planned stroke, touch and palette trip
  priced in hand time; with `c.set_hand_time(..)` the paint ages while the
  hand works, a long pass in slices: `notes/time.md`
- `bristle` – simulated brushes (round, flat, filbert, fan, rigger, badger):
  per-bristle reservoirs, bend and splay, contact with the surface relief,
  deposit, pickup and ploughing (each hair ploughs by its own size, so a
  stroke over dry paint covers its middle: `notes/fixes/dry_rims/`); a round or rigger given a point
  (`Tool::point`, opt-in) paints a hairline with the point, spread with pressure and lift off to a
  point, the same at any resolution (`notes/tip.md`)
- `handling` – how a painter covers an area: hand-like stroke planning (arcs,
  criss-cross, drift, dabs, broken strokes, pressure swell; see
  `notes/strokes.md`), passage-by-passage or swept order, trips to the
  palette, parallel tiles with exact pixel footprints
- `style` – painter profiles: support, grounds, tools, handling (from sourced
  knowledge, see `notes/research/`)
- `hand` – writing small motifs as brush gestures in a local frame
- `graphite` – the underdrawing: graphite grades and black chalk dragged over
  the ground's tooth, in the picture under the paint (thin paint shows it,
  body color hides it), a kneaded eraser and fixative: `notes/pencil.md`
- `pigment` – Kubelka–Munk layers (Curtis et al. 1997); `color` – Mixbox, OKLab
- `crack` – craquelure grown crack by crack from film stress (T-junctions,
  weave-following on thin grounds, cupping, grime); each crack opens by
  the stress it released (first cracks widest), `grain` gives a dominant
  direction, `vary`/`patchy` make it uneven. Alice's lab and what's
  still off: `notes/cracks_lab/README.md`
- `palette` – the painter's tubes and mixing on the palette; what a paint's
  color means (masstone vs. the look on the canvas): `notes/color.md`
- `stipple` – many small touches of a brush tip (Friedrich's skies, mist,
  distant hills), each simulated through the bristles: `notes/stipple.md`
- `form` – the painter's model of a solid: a depth buffer of bodies (`Sdf`
  ellipsoids and blocks, turned, cut and weathered), reliefs and mountain
  faces (`Ridge`), lit with cast shadows. It gives per-point planes, light
  and shadow families, fall lines and masks for parts, facets, silhouettes
  and edges. It paints nothing: `notes/form.md`
- `scene` – one world, one sun: a camera (horizon, ground plane, scale at
  depth), ground and water, bodies placed on the ground, cast shadows traced
  along the sun, contact seams, mirror images in still or rippled water,
  ribbons and spacing that recede. Every `Form` in it is lit alike. It
  paints nothing: `notes/scene.md`
- `atmos` – the air for the same sun: a physical sky (single scattering,
  ozone, the Earth's shadow and Belt of Venus, uneven haze, haze layers,
  overcast) sampled as paint over a camera; cloud volumes (cumulus, banks,
  decks with breaks) lit by the sun, as fields (alpha, lit edge, belly,
  silver lining, edge softness); receding ranges at uneven distances with
  varied silhouettes and stratified haze. It paints nothing:
  `notes/atmosphere.md`
- `canvas` – glazes, relief lighting, dithered PNG out
- `growth` – how trees grow (buds, light, vigor, pipe-model widths, decline):
  returns a skeleton of limbs, including which parts are dead wood;
  leaves as lit clumps on the young wood (`Skeleton::foliage`: masks,
  light, sky gaps) and meadow tufts in perspective and wind (`Sward`);
  painting them is the painter's job: `notes/motifs.md`, `notes/green.md`
- `mask`, `edge`, `shape`, `path`, `noise`, `rng` – geometry and randomness

# Caspar David Friedrich: painting materials and technique

*Process and hand (sequence, studies and their transfer, edges, pace, what copies got wrong) are in `friedrich_process.md`.*

*Sourced technical report for a physical paint simulator. Every claim cites a source key; full URLs are in the "Sources" list at the end. "Uncertain" marks claims that are unverified, disputed or taken from a single object.*

## Bottom line

Friedrich painted in oil on fine, plain-weave linen that he bought already primed. The grounds had two to four thin layers: a warm lower layer (red or ocher) under a light, lead-white-rich top layer [KÖR p.284; CATS p.127]. Over a precise graphite or ink underdrawing he laid a very thin underpainting, then only one or two very thin paint layers [SMB-proj; CATS p.127]. He used few pigments. Before about 1820 his key blue was smalt, a semi-transparent cobalt glass. After that he used cobalt blue and chrome yellow [ALF pp.341, 348–349]. His smooth gradations come from stippling and from paint pooling in the fine texture of the ground, not from thick blending [CATS p.127; NG p.56]. No accessible source gives numeric thread counts or paint-film thicknesses in microns for his paintings. The simulator values below for those are labeled proxies or assumptions.

**Terms used below.** *Ground/priming*: the preparatory layers between canvas and paint. *Cross-section*: a microscopic sample cut through all layers. *IRR (infrared reflectography)*: imaging that shows carbon-based drawing under paint. *XRF (X-ray fluorescence)*: elemental analysis. *Glaze*: a transparent paint layer. *Impasto*: thick, raised paint. *Lining*: gluing a second canvas to the back. *Craquelure*: the network of cracks in paint or varnish.

## 1. Supports

- **Fabric.** The Berlin *Monk by the Sea* and *Abbey in the Oakwood* are on "fine linen canvas." Both canvases were cut from adjoining sections of one roll, which was established by thread-count weave matching [CATS p.127 and n.2]. The Dresden paintings use locally grown flax, handwoven in plain weave. In his late work Friedrich preferred "finer, more densely woven canvases" [KÖR p.283].
- **One piece of cloth.** He used a single strip of canvas regardless of size, so even large formats have no seams [KÖR p.283].
- **Thread count.** No numeric count for any Friedrich canvas appeared in accessible sources. Mösl's 2021 dissertation and a 2024–25 journal double issue on 48 paintings probably contain them [ART; SKD]. **Proxy:** the Danish painter Eckersberg, who also bought ready-primed Dresden canvas (1827–34), painted his post-1816 Danish works on canvases of 10–16 threads/cm in both directions [CATS-E pp.45–47].
- **Sizes.** From 32.5 × 45 cm (*Winter Landscape*) [RSC p.42] to 110.6 × 171.4 cm (*Monk*) [CATS p.126].
- **Stretching.** The most common stretcher type in his work is softwood with blind mortise-and-tenon corners and hardwood wedges [KÖR p.283]. Uneven pull marks ("cusping") on only one edge of *Winter Landscape* suggest the piece was cut from a larger, already-primed length [NG pp.51, 55].
- **Panels.** None of the sources I consulted document panel supports for his oils. *Uncertain.*

## 2. Grounds (preparation layers)

- **Commercial, multi-layer and warm underneath.** Friedrich used commercially primed canvas cut from long lengths. Dresden suppliers sold primed cloth in several colors [KÖR p.284]. Dresden grounds have **two to four thin layers** [KÖR p.284]. Lower layers contain inexpensive ocher, burnt red earth, chalk and barium sulfate and "only served to smooth and even out the weave texture." Upper layers are dominated by lead white, probably bound in oil, and Friedrich painted mostly on "a patchy whitish ground" [KÖR p.284].
- **Berlin pair.** Three priming layers: bright red, then two light brown. The first two were applied with a spatula. The third looks roller-applied and has "a finely textured structure" that Friedrich exploited [CATS p.127; SMB-blog]. In a sky cross-section of *Abbey*, the red preparation contains aluminosilicate and iron oxides. It is followed by several yellow-gray lead-white layers containing iron oxides, vermilion grains and calcium-rich grains [NPJ25].
- **London *Winter Landscape*.** Two layers, both chalk and lead white with a little umber and ocher. The upper layer has more lead white, so it is lighter and cooler. The binder is walnut oil [NG p.55].
- **Tool marks.** X-rays show wavy strokes from priming knives in the lower layers. The top layer was brushed, and its bristle striations "shine through the thin upper paint layers" and are visible to the naked eye [KÖR p.284].
- **Colored grounds by motif.** *Two Men Contemplating the Moon* (Dresden) has a reddish-ocher top ground that serves as the mid-tone and stays visible under loose paint [KÖR p.284]. In *The Sea of Ice* a pink or reddish ground shows through the sky and is left bare in places [HH].
- **Weave visibility.** The lower ground layers level the weave [KÖR p.284]. The visible micro-texture comes mainly from the top ground (brush striations or roller texture), not from the weave.
- **Thickness.** No micron values were found. *Gap.*

## 3. Underdrawing

- **Media.** Graphite pencils of different hardness and black chalk, sometimes in two passes: a faint first outline, then a bolder one. Ruled lines were probably drawn against a ruler [CATS pp.128, 131]. Carus described chalk and pencil first, then "quill-pen and ink" [CATS p.132; NG p.49]. In *Winter Landscape*, faint ruled lines (possibly pencil) sit under thicker ink lines [NG pp.49, 58].
- **Change over his career.** Early works are drawn almost entirely in graphite, and the drawing often stays visible through the extremely thin paint. From 1811 to the mid- or late 1820s a pen is added and the paint gets denser. Late works use a pointed brush, and the drawing is almost fully covered [ART, summarizing Mösl 2021].
- **Precision.** "Rich in detail," with "no gradation of detail according to significance" [CATS p.132]. Friedrich often *removed* drawn motifs during painting. *Monk* has three drawn ships that were never painted [CATS p.128].
- **Visible through paint.** Lines "still partly shimmer through" [CATS p.132]. Drawn dune and grass zigzags show through in *Monk* [CATS p.130]. Traces of the drawing appear as dark dots at color boundaries in *The Sea of Ice* [HH].
- **Exception.** Infrared found no underdrawing in the Met's *Two Men Contemplating the Moon* (c.1825–30) [MET PDF pp.19, 45].
- **Tools.** Kersting's 1811 picture of Friedrich's studio shows two palettes, a set square, a T-square, a ruler and a maulstick [KÖR/Busch pp.326–327].

## 5. Binding media and additives

- **Walnut oil** in both ground and paint of *Winter Landscape* [NG p.55]. This is the only published medium analysis I found. Linseed or poppy oil, resins and driers are *unverified* for Friedrich.
- **Egg white** as a temporary coating (see section 7) [CATS p.127; KÖR p.283].

## 6. Layer structure and application

- **Number of layers.** "One to two very thin layers" of paint [SMB-proj]. *Abbey*: primings 1–3, underdrawing, underpainting, one smalt paint layer, egg white, then later varnishes [CATS fig. 3]. *Monk*: a first dark-blue layer, then light blue, pink and white over the central sky [CATS p.127]. *Winter Landscape*: "a single thin layer using remarkably few pigments" [NG p.56]. *The Cross in the Mountains* (1807/08) sky: two ocher ground layers, a patchy white ground, a thin violet layer (smalt splinters and cinnabar), then a very thin pale-yellow layer [KÖR fig. 6].
- **Film thickness.** Described as "very, very fine layers" [SPK] and a "gossamer-thin film" [CATS p.127]. No micron values were found. *Gap.*
- **The pooling effect.** The thin paint "accumulated in the depths of the textured ground layers," producing the finest dots of color. That let him avoid visible brushstrokes and get "almost continuous gradations" [CATS p.127].
- **Stippling.** Skies, mist and distant hills are stippled, which "enhance[s] the transparency and light scattering" [NG p.56]. The moon sky of *Two Men Contemplating the Moon* is stippled [KÖR fig. 7].
- **Strokes.** Early brushwork is "painstaking… small strokes of paint placed side by side like a closely woven textile." Firs are done in short hatched strokes [NG pp.49–50]. Grass is done with "fine upturning" strokes laid over the finished snow [NG p.56].
- **Impasto.** In early works it is limited, for example the slight impasto of foreground snow [NG p.50]. *The Sea of Ice* mixes thick and thin paint and leaves the ground bare in places [HH].
- **Order of work.** Ground (bought), then underdrawing, then a "very thin underpainting," then paint [CATS p.127]. Details go on last: grass over snow [NG p.56]; twenty small gulls were added to the completed *Monk* [CATS p.130]. Brush types (sable or bristle) are *undocumented* in these sources.
- **Glazing.** Friedrich told Carus to lay a dark glaze over a whole moonlit picture except the moon, "growing darker toward the picture's edges" [MET PDF p.35]. This is advice to another painter, not an analysis of his own paintings.

## 7. Varnish

- **Original coating.** Egg white. Friedrich's letters say he coated fresh paintings with a temporary egg-white film. Buyers were to wash it off and apply a mastic resin varnish within a year [KÖR p.283]. Egg-white remains were detected on *Abbey* [CATS p.127] and on Dresden's *View over the Elbe Valley* [KÖR p.283].
- **Later coatings.** *Monk* and *Abbey* had up to **seven** yellowed varnish layers. Parts of them had fine microcracks whose edges reflected light "like a milky veil" [SMB-blog]. *Winter Landscape* had yellowed dammar, possibly with copaiba balsam residues [NG p.55]. The Hamburg *Sea of Ice* was lined in 1938 [HH].

## 8. Condition and aging

- **Fragility.** The thin paint made the paintings "exceptionally prone to damage" [SMB-proj]. Numerous micro-losses come from abrasion during past cleaning [SMB-blog].
- **Smalt discoloration.** In *Abbey*, smalt has partly lost its color. Low potassium (4.9 wt%) and changes in cobalt coordination show it is in an intermediate stage of degradation. A simulation of the original colors comes out cooler and bluer [NPJ25; SMB-blog]. Smalt can turn brown over time [HH].
- **Lining damage.** The 1906 wax-resin lining of *Monk* and *Abbey* left lumps, iron marks and ground and paint damage [SMB-blog]. Restoration (2013–16) found about 97% (*Monk*) and 98% (*Abbey*) of the original paint surviving [SMB-blog].
- **Craquelure.** *The Sea of Ice* has an elongated "ear-of-grain-shaped" craquelure, probably from pressure on the back [HH]. No quantitative crack study of a Friedrich painting was found. **Generic mechanics:** corner cracks form perpendicular to the diagonal within about 5–10% of the diagonal length. A mock-up corner showed about 6 ± 3 mm crack spacing. Central cracks come from isotropic drying shrinkage of the oil paint [NPJ24].
- **Pentimenti** (the painter's own changes). Few in *Winter Landscape* [NG p.49]. The turned figure in *Monk* is a rare case [ART; CATS p.129].

## 9. Greens

*Same conventions as sections 1–8: source keys in brackets, full URLs in the source list below. "Unverified" means I could not see the primary text myself.*

**Bottom line.** Friedrich's greens were mostly **mixed on the palette** from his blues and yellows. He also used two or three true green pigments sparingly. The Dresden team (14 paintings) writes, in my translation, that "the palette was very sparing" but his greens show a "lush variety" ("üppige Vielfalt"). They list the true greens as "copper-containing pigments and green earth." He "often mixed his green from blue and yellow," using Prussian blue "very often" and smalt and cobalt blue as well. The yellow part came from yellow ocher, Naples yellow or chrome yellow [MÄD p.102]. Green passages often have "several (up to four) layers of different greens" stacked on top of each other [MÄD p.102].

### Evidence in Friedrich's paintings

- **Winter Landscape (London, c.1811), grass.** The grass has no true green pigment: "smalt, Naples yellow, bone black, ochre and possibly Prussian blue in varying proportions" [NG p.56]. Section 4 omits the smalt; it should be added to the grass list.
- **Dresden, 14 paintings.** Copper greens and green earth were used; mixtures were frequent (see the bottom line above) [MÄD p.102]. The abstract does not say which paintings or dates contain green earth. *Gap.*
- **Bohemian Landscape with the Milleschauer (1808, Dresden)** [CDF-M]. XRF found Cu plus As, and SEM-EDX placed both in the same layer. Spectroscopy found no intact copper arsenite, so the authors assume a "degraded form" of Scheele's or Schweinfurt green [MÄD p.102]. *Single object.* **My inference:** since 1808 predates Schweinfurt green (1814), this would be Scheele's green unless the layer is a later addition.
- **Rinmann's green, rare.** Found by the Doerner Institut on *Riesengebirgslandschaft mit aufsteigendem Nebel* (c.1819/20) [PIN], by SPSG on *Ländliche ebene Gegend* (c.1822/23) and in Dresden on *Hünengrab im Herbst* (c.1820) [MÄD p.102 n.3; CDF-H]. The SPSG/Hannover study says his mixed greens were supplemented by "the rarely detectable Rinmann's green and a copper green" [MOST-abs].
- **Unverified (search-tool summary of the Most 2024 PDF, which I could not open; page not seen).** In *Ländliche ebene Gegend*, Rinmann's green reportedly lies in a light, pastose top layer applied in short dabs or zigzags over a yellow-green layer. An arsenic-free copper green reportedly appears in the green reflections of boats in *Ansicht eines Hafens*. Check these before use.
- **Berlin, four paintings.** XRF covered only blue and yellow areas. "No Cu was detected in any investigated area" means blue areas only, not greens [ALF pp.346, 348].
- **A cautionary misattribution.** *Landschaft mit kahlem Baum* was de-attributed partly because its leaves are cobalt blue mixed with chrome yellow, which were anachronistic for 1798/99 [MÄD p.102]. The pigment date rule works as a real test.
- **No green data found** for *Hill and Ploughed Field*, *Meadows near Greifswald*, *Morning in the Riesengebirge*, *Chalk Cliffs*, *Lone Tree* or *Summer*. The ZKK 2024–25 issues are paywalled; page not seen.

### How he painted foliage and grass

- **Order.** Trees were painted "on the already painted sky" [ALF p.346]. Grass came last, as "fine upturning" strokes over the finished snow [NG p.56].
- **Strokes.** Firs are "short, hatched strokes" [NG pp.49–50]. The SPSG study notes that he modeled paint while it was still wet ("die noch nicht getrocknete Farbe modellierte") [MOST-abs]. In *Woman before the Setting Sun* the grass blades are straight, made with "a stiff, inflexible paint brush" and probably applied last. The author calls them "entirely unique in Friedrich's oeuvre" [UCL pp.116–117].
- **Drawing habits.** His foliage drawings use "small strokes and hooks" and "jagged lines." He noted distance and viewpoint on the sheet [KH, publisher excerpt; exact page uncertain]. He studied grasses and plants in dated pencil sketches (1799, 1806–07) [KSW].
- **Contemporaries.** Carus mocked painters who "confound all the specific forms of tree growth in an imaginary substance that they call 'foliage'" [CAR p.137]. Field's rule for landscape greens was to mix them from the yellows of the foreground and the blues of the sky, because they "harmonize better… and impart homogeneity" [FIELD p.128]. For Goethe, green is yellow and blue balanced, a color on which "the eye and the mind repose" [GOE §802].

### Recommendation for the simulator palette

**Early (pre-1820).** Add **Prussian blue** (S: "sehr häufig" in greens [MÄD p.102]; "possibly" in grass [NG p.56]) and **green earth** (S [MÄD p.102], dates unassigned). By default, build greens by mixing: smalt or Prussian blue + ochre or Naples yellow + bone black [NG p.56]. **Optional:** a "copper green" tube, flagged rare.

**Post-1820.** Keep the early additions. Cobalt blue + chrome yellow mixes become possible with tubes you already have. Add **Rinmann's green** as a rare tube (three objects, c.1819–1823).

**Leave out:**
- Viridian (1859/1863) and chromium oxide (1845+) [AP3 p.275]
- Emerald green as a standard tube: it was secret until 1822 and poor in oil [AP3 p.222; FIELD p.130]. Keep at most a "degraded Cu-As green" special case (single object)
- A ready-made *Zinnobergrün* tube: there is no Friedrich evidence, so mix it instead
- Sap green: "totally useless" in oil [FIELD p.131]

Rendering: allow up to four stacked green layers [MÄD p.102]. Paint foliage after the sky and grass last.

**In the simulator** (`Palette::friedrich_early_greens`, `friedrich_1820_greens`, `copper_green`; notes/green.md): Prussian blue and green earth join both periods, Rinmann's green the post-1820 one, copper green as an optional rare tube. The base palettes are kept without them (the aimed search picked Prussian blue for skies).

# Trees in Friedrich's world: how they are built and how he used them

*Sourced note for painters who work from knowledge, not pictures. Companion to `friedrich_materials.md` (materials) and `friedrich_process.md` (process). Every claim carries a source key in brackets; full URLs are in "Sources" at the end. "General knowledge" marks botanical statements I could not tie to a source I read. "My inference" marks conclusions I drew from sourced facts. "Unverified" marks claims I saw only secondhand. Rule kept throughout: no picture of his was looked at; descriptions of his works come from museum, catalog and scholarly text only.*

## Bottom line

1. **A tree is a branching system that grows at its tips and thickens everywhere.** Strong side branches arise mostly near the top of each year's shoot (acrotony). Upright axes build the frame; side axes spread sideways. When a tip dies, the one or more side shoots below it take over, so the axis forks or zigzags [BC pp.381–387].
2. **Diameter is conserved across forks, roughly.** The cross-section below a fork about equals the sum of the cross-sections above it (Leonardo's rule). The measured exponent is 1.8–2.3 instead of exactly 2 [ELOY p.1; MT p.1]. Every twig is the thin end of a continuous path to the roots [LEH].
3. **A side branch is thickest where it leaves its parent.** It is set into the trunk as a sleeve: the branch's own wood turns down and wraps its base as a collar, and trunk wood wraps over that collar every year [SHIGO]. A swelling underneath (the branch collar) and usually a raised ridge of bark on top (the branch bark ridge) mark the junction [USDA p.10].
4. **Healthy crowns end in a network of long shoots; stressed ones don't.** Roloff's four vitality stages run from a net of long shoots at the crown edge (healthy) to spiky "bottle-brush" tips, then bushy chains of short shoots, then dieback and a shrinking crown [ROL17]. He rates each stage against the tree's age, and asks when the short-shoot stage is simply normal in old oaks [ROL17].
5. **Old trees shrink downward rather than simply dying.** An ancient oak loses its upper crown and keeps a live, often dense lower crown. It becomes "stag-headed," with dead limbs standing above the living foliage, and usually hollow [ATF; HTC; WT].
6. **A pollard willow is a thick trunk cut at 2–4 m with a swollen knuckle (the "head") on top.** Many rods sprout from just below the old cut [DVL]. On a vigorous tree they can grow 1.5–2.5 m in a year [LOGAN]. Rods were harvested every one to ten years, depending on use. Pollards left uncut too long split apart under their heavy limbs [DVL; BL].
7. **Snow sticks best near 0 °C.** Adhesion rises as the air warms toward freezing, and cold dry snow is shaken off bare trees [MIL64 pp.5–6]. Snow lies in bands on smooth bark and in heaps on rough bark [MIL64 p.6]. It slides off sloping or bent supports and lets go first where it touches the branch [MIL66]. Rime (Raueis) grows into the wind; hoarfrost (Raureif) is fragile needles formed in calm, humid cold [DWD].
8. **Friedrich built his trees from dated pencil studies of individual trees, reused for decades.** Roughly 400 of about 1300 drawings put trees at the center, mostly oaks and spruces [ROL]. One 1809 oak study served paintings from 1811 to about 1835 [MET PDF p.37]. He drew with a horizon line marked even on the lower trunk and kept that viewpoint in the painting [BUSCH-V pp.77–78].
9. **Pollard willows:** yes, in at least one painting; he also made several willow studies. *The Hut in the Snow* (1827) shows willows that one scholar calls "pollard willows" [UCL p.26]. The museum text describes their "vigorous young shoots" [CDF-HÜT]. Willow studies are dated 1799, 1808, 1809 and 1812. One tree biologist reports that pictures of lopped trees are nearly absent from his work [ROL]. Details in §5.6.

**Terms used below.** *Acrotony*: side branches strongest near the tip of the parent shoot. *Orthotropic/plagiotropic*: growing upright/growing sideways. *Long shoot/short shoot*: a year's extension that is long and carries branches versus a stubby one. *Epicormic shoot*: a shoot from a dormant bud on an old trunk or limb (German *Wasserreiser*). *Reiteration*: the tree repeating its own basic architecture as a new sub-crown [BC pp.390–391]. *Retrenchment*: natural shrinking of an old crown [ATF]. *Stag-headed*: dead top limbs standing above a live lower crown [HTC]. *Pollard*: tree cut back repeatedly at head height. *Bolling/head*: the permanent trunk and knuckle of a pollard. *Rods*: the shoots from the head. *Cladoptosis*: a tree's regular shedding of twigs at an abscission layer [WP-CLAD]. *Sapwood/heartwood*: conducting outer wood/non-conducting inner wood. *Raureif/Raueis*: hoarfrost/rime.

## 1. How a tree is built

- **Growth rules.** Branches that develop mostly in the distal part of a parent shoot (acrotony) are what give a tree its tree-like rather than bushy habit [BC pp.383–384]. Upright (orthotropic) axes "are generally associated with plant skeleton construction." Sideways (plagiotropic) axes explore horizontal space and carry leaves and flowers [BC p.385]. If a shoot's tip dies, aborts or turns into a flower, one, two or more branches take over below it (sympodial branching). A string of such takeovers can still look like one straight axis [BC pp.381–382].
- **Branch order.** The trunk (order 1) bears branches (order 2), which bear their own (order 3), and so on. In sympodial systems the order climbs fast [BC p.382]. **General knowledge:** a mature broadleaved crown commonly has five or more orders from trunk to current-year twig. I found no source that counts them species by species.
- **The tree repeats itself.** As a crown matures, the tree builds new sub-crowns that duplicate its own architecture on big limbs. This "sequential" reiteration is a normal part of crown construction [BC p.391]. After damage, dormant buds produce "traumatic" reiteration: new sub-crowns on the wounded frame [BC p.390].
- **Long shoots and short shoots set the crown edge.** In a vigorous tree the leader and some side shoots at the top are long shoots, making a "network structure" that extends the crown. Next comes a "spikey outline," with bottle-brush tips of long leaders carrying only short side shoots. Then a "short shoot-mode" with "bushy structure, on hold." Last is "retraction mode": "leader die-back, crown reduction" [ROL17]. Roloff measured these stages on 100- to 160-year-old beech [ROL17]. He sorts species by life expectancy. Short-lived (80–100 years) includes alder and birch. Medium-lived (150–300) includes beech, spruce, pine and white willow. Long-lived (over 400) includes lime and oak [ROL17].
- **What distress looks like.** In an ancient tree the outer crown shrinks episodically, and new epicormic shoots grow in the mid and lower crown [WT]. Old trees survive through epicormic growth, adventitious rooting, layering and suckering [WT]. *My inference:* a crown whose every limb is covered in straight upright shoots reads as a tree reacting to heavy damage or cutting. A healthy mature crown edge is a fine net of long shoots.

## 2. How branches taper and join

- **Leonardo's rule.** Leonardo wrote that "all the branches of a tree at every stage of its height when put together are equal in thickness to the trunk." In modern terms, a mother branch of diameter *d* splitting into daughters *dᵢ* obeys *d*^Δ = Σ *dᵢ*^Δ on average. Measured Δ is between 1.8 and 2.3 for many species (Δ = 2 means cross-sectional area is conserved) [ELOY p.1]. *Arithmetic from the rule:* with Δ = 2, two equal daughters are each about 0.71 of the mother's diameter. A daughter with a quarter of the area has half the diameter, and the mother continuing past it drops only to about 0.87 of its former diameter.
- **Why: two explanations.** The *pipe model* (Shinozaki et al. 1964) pictures a tree as a bundle of unit pipes, each connecting a set of leaves to the roots. So the stem area at a height tracks the leaves above it [LEH]. Below the crown, the pipes of branches long since shed stay in the trunk as "disused pipes." That is why trunks keep thickening toward the base even where no branches remain [LEH, quoting Shinozaki]. Eloy objects that the conducting sapwood can be as little as 5% of a mature trunk's cross-section [ELOY p.1]. He shows instead that Leonardo's rule follows if a self-similar tree skeleton sizes its diameters to resist wind [ELOY]. Whatever the cause, cross-sections sum roughly at forks [LEH; MT].
- **When the rule bends.** Models depart from the rule as side branches get heavier or leave at wider angles. In real branches the departure is small. Beech branches fit a constant-stress design best; fir branches often follow Leonardo's rule [MT p.1]. *My inference:* a heavy, near-horizontal limb is somewhat thicker at its base than the area rule alone would give.
- **What a junction is.** The cambium runs continuously from trunk to branch. In the upper junction, though, its cells are oriented at "approximately right angles" to the normal direction. Early in the season the branch xylem turns downward at the branch base and "encircles it to form a collar." Later in the season a collar of trunk xylem envelops it. "The branch is structurally attached to the trunk by a series of trunk collars that envelop the branch collars every growing season." Water enters and leaves the branch through the branch collar [SHIGO]. Outwardly there is a branch collar on the underside of the branch base and a branch bark ridge on top, running roughly parallel to the branch angle [USDA p.10].
- **Why a side branch never starts thinner than it is farther out.** *My inference, from [LEH] and [SHIGO]:* at its base a branch carries the pipes for every leaf beyond it, and each year's collar adds wood there first. Its cross-section therefore shrinks outward, stepwise at each fork and gradually between forks, and never the other way. A branch drawn as a constant-width rod, or narrower where it leaves the trunk, contradicts both.
- **Angle of attachment.** Wide, U-shaped unions are strong. Narrow V-shaped unions "often form included bark," a wedge of inward-rolled bark between two stems. Codominant stems of about equal size from one point often do the same [USDA p.6]. When a leader is damaged, several branches may become codominant [USDA p.7].
- **Dead branches and stubs.** Around a dead branch, the collar and branch bark ridge "continue to grow" and can be told apart from the dead wood [USDA p.13]. *General knowledge:* over years a living collar can form a sleeve around a dead stub.
- **Twigs end in buds.** Each twig is the current year's shoot and ends in a terminal or false-terminal bud. Buds sit in the leaf scars along it (species details in §3) [VT]. Nothing in a tree floats. Every twig connects through its parent to the trunk, as the pipe model presumes [LEH].

## 3. The species

### 3.1 Oak (*Quercus robur*, pedunculate; *Q. petraea*, sessile)

- **Habit.** In *Q. robur* the main trunk "tends to disappear in the crown, developing irregular boughs with twisting branches." *Q. petraea* usually keeps a main stem with boughs that gradually decrease in size [JRC-Q]. Heights are usually about 30 m, with diameters up to 1 m. Individuals can live over 1000 years and reach 3–4 m in diameter [JRC-Q]. The crown is round [VT oak].
- **Twigs and buds.** Twigs are moderate in thickness and yellow-brown. Buds are "angled, short and round" [VT oak]. **General knowledge:** oak buds cluster at the shoot tip, so several shoots start from one point, which gives oak its crooked, clustered branching.
- **Twig shedding (cladoptosis).** In cladoptosis an abscission layer forms and the twig "is shed cleanly," as leaves are [WP-CLAD]. In oak, most shed twigs are one year old and leafless. They fall in autumn and mostly come from vigorously growing trees, so the shedding is not a sign of drought or age [RUST]. In a 165-year-old stand, weak shoots had 27% lower hydraulic conductance, with bottlenecks at nodes and abscission zones [RR02].
- **Bark.** Gray and fissured into rectangular elongated blocks, thicker in *Q. robur* [JRC-Q]. "Deeply fissured with age" [VT oak].
- **Old and damaged oaks.** Oaks coppice and pollard easily. Lateral epicormic shoots leave knots in the wood [JRC-Q]. Ancient oaks retrench: the crown shrinks through dieback and branch loss ("growing downwards"). The trunk is very wide for the species and very likely hollow, and the tree may live on for centuries [ATF]. "Stagheaded oaks are classic examples of early stage retrenchment" [HTC]. In natural retrenchment, single branches die back while the rest of the crown stays healthy. Serious disease looks different [ATF].
- **Winter and leaf.** A museum text on Friedrich's *Oak Tree in Snow* (1829) describes the tree still carrying the previous year's brown leaves, which it drops only when new leaves grow in spring [CDF-EICH]. **General knowledge:** young and lower oak branches often keep dead leaves through winter (marcescence); old crowns do so less.

### 3.2 Beech (*Fagus sylvatica*)

- **Habit.** Usually single-stemmed, with silver-gray bark. Typical life span 150–300 years. It keeps growing fast into late maturity and is the most shade-tolerant broadleaf in its range [JRC-F]. A stocky trunk and round crown [VT beech].
- **Twigs and buds.** Twigs are "slender, zigzag, light brown." Buds are long (about 2.5 cm), slender and "widely divergent from stems" [VT beech]. Beech was Roloff's model species for the long-shoot/short-shoot vitality stages [ROL17].
- **Bark.** "Smooth, thin, and dark gray-blue … smooth even on the largest stems, may be mottled" [VT beech]. The thin bark protects poorly against fire and stripping [JRC-F].
- **Taper.** Japanese beech branches fit a uniform-stress design best [MT p.1].

### 3.3 Birch (*Betula pendula*, silver; *B. pubescens*, downy)

- **Habit.** Short-lived (commonly 90–100 years, rarely 150), relatively small, with a light canopy [JRC-B]. The crown is open and pyramidal, "with distinctly drooping fine branches" [VT birch]. In *B. pendula* the branches droop; in *B. pubescens* they grow upward or horizontally [JRC-B].
- **Twigs.** "Slender, reddish brown … noticeably drooping," with slender pointed buds [VT birch].
- **Bark.** Brown when young, then "silvery-white, with horizontal dark grey lenticels, that with age darkens and develops fissures." Young trees show dark scars where shoots dropped [JRC-B]. At the base the tree "develops thick bark which splits into narrow, vertical furrows which are nearly black" [VT birch].

### 3.4 Lime (*Tilia cordata*, small-leaved; *T. platyphyllos*, large-leaved)

- **Habit.** 30–40 m, with straight trunks up to about 1 m. Crowns are "quite neat and narrow, becoming untidier as they age," with a branch-free trunk of 10–15 m possible. Both species are largely free of suckers and epicormic growth, unlike the hybrid common lime [JRC-T]. Open-grown trees are dense and round, and become as wide as tall [VT lime].
- **Twigs and buds.** "Slender, zigzag, green-brown or red-tinged (particularly in the winter)." The terminal bud is false; buds are plump with one side bulging [VT lime].
- **Bark.** Gray or brown, with shallow furrows and flat ridges [VT lime]. "Numerous burls and sprouts often found around the base" [VT lime].
- **Old limes.** They live over 1000 years even when coppiced. Very old stools may have lost their heartwood to rot [JRC-T]. Limes were coppiced for long straight poles [JRC-T] and can be pollarded [BL].

### 3.5 Willow (white willow, *Salix alba*; other tree willows) and the pollard

- **The tree.** A fast-growing tree of riverbanks and floodplains, very tolerant of flooding. It can be pollarded or coppiced, and it "can readily reproduce from suckers or from adventitious roots" [JRC-S]. The bark is dark gray and deeply fissured with corky ridges. The narrow leaves are silver-gray, and white willow is "cultivated as osiers, characterised by having pliable branches" [JRC-S]. Medium-lived [ROL17]. Willows used as pollards include white, hybrid crack (*S. rubens*), crack (*S. fragilis*) and basket (*S. viminalis*) willow [DVL; NM].
- **How a pollard is made.** The trunk is cut through at 2 to 4 m. The tree then resprouts "vieltriebig" (in many shoots) from buds just below the cut, and repeated cutting thickens that place into the "head" [DVL]. While the tree is being trained, all side shoots on the trunk are removed except in the top 10–20 cm, and the head grows from those [NM]. In the 2nd to 4th year, 40–60% of the new shoots are cut back to about 5 cm, mostly the suppressed ones [DVL].
- **Rods: age, use and number.** Traditionally the thin rods were taken one to two years after cutting, for baskets, fish traps and house building. The rest were thinned after three to five years for tool handles. Whatever remained was left until about the tenth year for firewood, and then the whole head was cut again [DVL]. Tall pollards are cut every 3–5 years and carry "a gnarled head and thick, several-year-old branches." Low basket willows are cut every year [BL]. Old pollards should be cut only about every 5 years, and a cut is overdue once the branches are 10 cm thick [BL]. Poles over 5 cm thick are heavy [DVL]. **Number of rods:** I found no source that gives a count per head. The sources say "many shoots" and describe thinning by half [DVL]. **Growth:** "on a vigorous willow five to eight feet of growth in a year is not uncommon," and cut sprouts are replaced in the same year [LOGAN].
- **How rods stand and bend.** No source I read describes rod angles. *General knowledge:* new rods on a pollard head grow nearly vertical at first. As they lengthen and age over several years they lean outward under their own weight, so old uncut heads spread. White willow's "pliable branches" [JRC-S] bend under load without breaking. Logan describes Somerset pollards as "like shocks of hair, others like a sack thrown over the trunk's back, and some like rows of Corinthian columns" [LOGAN].
- **Old pollards.** Heads develop holes, niches and cavities used by owls, other birds and bats. Trunks become hollow [DVL; BL]. Old pollards left uncut "threaten to break apart," because the trunk, especially a hollow one, can no longer carry the heavy branches [DVL].

### 3.6 Alder (*Alnus glutinosa*, black alder)

- **Habit.** Short-lived (normally about 60 years, maximum about 160), 10–25 m, on riverbanks, lake shores and marshes [JRC-A]. The crown is narrow and upright [VT alder]. Shaded branches die off, so the live crown shrinks relative to the tree [JRC-A]. It can be coppiced [JRC-A].
- **Twigs and winter features.** Young twigs are green and sticky. Buds are stalked, purplish brown and somewhat three-sided [VT alder]. Catkins form in autumn and open the next spring. The fruits are small woody "cones" that stay on through winter and release seed gradually [JRC-A; VT alder].
- **Bark.** Brown and smooth at first, then darker, rough and fissured [JRC-A]. Later gray-brown with small broken patches [VT alder].
- **Damage.** *Phytophthora* disease kills first the fine branches, then the larger ones [JRC-A].

### 3.7 Norway spruce (*Picea abies*)

- **Habit.** A straight, regular trunk up to 50–60 m, usually living 200–300 years [JRC-PA]. "The crown is regularly conic, columnar, with whorled, short and stout branches, the upper level ascending and the lower drooping" [JRC-PA]. Free-standing trees keep green branches down to the ground [WP-FI]. Branches are inclined to hanging, as an adaptation to snow load [WP-FI].
- **Branching types.** Young spruces branch in flat "plates" up to about 20 years. After that they develop either the *Plattenfichte* type, with horizontal second-order branches, or the *Kammfichte* ("comb spruce") type, whose second- and higher-order branches hang down like a fringe. A third type is the *Bürstenfichte* ("brush spruce") [WP-FI]. Comb spruces dominate on well-supplied sites. Plate spruces dominate on poor bogs and at extreme altitudes [WP-FI].
- **Bark.** Orange-brown [JRC-PA]. Red-brown and scaly, later gray with flaking scales or plates [VT spruce]. Drops of resin are common on trunk and branches [JRC-PA].
- **Spruce and fir.** A Hamburg catalog entry notes that spruce and fir are hard to tell apart even in nature, "all the more so painted in oil," and that Friedrich's *Early Snow* shows both [CDF-FRÜH]. Roloff finds that Friedrich usually distinguished them, but not always [ROL].

### 3.8 Scots pine (*Pinus sylvestris*)

- **Habit.** 23–27 m on average, sometimes over 40 m. It lives 400 years or more [JRC-PS]. Crowns are rounded when young and round-topped when old. The trunk is often twisted, depending on seed origin [VT pine]. In some conifers, flattening and broadening of the crown may be the only sign of old-age retrenchment [ATF].
- **Bark.** The upper stem is "a distinct reddish-orange," while the lower part is "furrowed brown to grey-brown and becomes deeply fissured" [JRC-PS]. "Upper crowns always show orange peeling bark" [VT pine].
- **Needles.** In pairs, twisted [VT pine]. Friedrich drew pine twigs with the paired needles botanically correct [ROL].

## 4. Snow and hoarfrost on bare trees

- **Bare trees do hold snow.** "Winter bareness of hardwoods may deceptively lead one to the assumption that they intercept no snow, when this is not true." Sheltered deciduous trees that are overtopped and out of the wind can hold snow on branches and forks as deep as on conifers, 20 cm [MIL64 p.7]. Measured over whole stands, deciduous forests kept up to 14% (average 11%) of snowfall, against an average 43% in conifer stands [HEL20 p.2557].
- **Temperature decides.** "Adhesion of snow to foliage presumably increases as temperature rises toward the freezing point." One Japanese series found interception rising about 30% of snowfall per degree Celsius of warming just below freezing [MIL64 p.5]. Storms in which a tree held little snow were cold, below −3 °C. "Dry snow in strong winds is generally intercepted less than wet snow" [MIL64 p.6]. Little dry snow stays in deciduous trees because they vibrate more, not because snow fails to hit them [MIL64 p.6]. *Unverified (abstract known only from secondary summaries):* on boards, catch below −3 °C rose with board width because crystals bounce off near edges. Above −3 °C cohesion made width irrelevant, and wet snow bridged gaps of 10 cm; board inclination and shape mattered [PS99].
- **Mechanisms.** Snow bridges between supports by cohesion, bounces off by elastic rebound, and is shed as branches bend. Light fluffy snow is caught best; catch falls as the snow gets denser [SG91].
- **Where it lies on a branch.** Bark texture matters: "snow forms in bands on deciduous trees if bark is smooth, in heaps if it is rough" [MIL64 p.6]. Wet snow driven by gales built up on the windward and upper halves of crowns [MIL64 p.3]. *My inference, from the above:* snow sits as a ridge along the upper side of limbs that are near horizontal and thick enough to stop bounce. Forks and crotches collect it. Steep limbs and thin, springy twigs hold little except in wet snow near 0 °C, which can bridge between twigs.
- **What falls off, and when.** Snow slides off branches "if the branches provide an unstable or slanting support." Loads balanced on branch ends bend them into steep slopes, which then release. Slight warming melts snow first at "the points of attachment to their supports," so masses slide off before they melt away [MIL66]. Wind shakes crowns, and deciduous trees lose snow mostly to that shaking, not to direct wind [MIL66].
- **Hoarfrost and rime (DWD definitions).** *Raureif* (hoarfrost) is "mostly thin, only loosely attached and fragile ice needles or scales," formed almost entirely by deposition from vapor. It needs humidity around 90% or more, weak wind and usually temperatures below −8 °C [DWD]. Its crystals are like snowflakes under a lens, often needle-shaped [DWD-T]. *Raueis* (rime) is a granular, "very firmly attached" deposit of supercooled fog droplets, milky white from trapped air. It forms mainly in fog at −2 to −10 °C, and strong wind favors it [DWD]. Its "ice flags" point into the wind [DWD-T]. *Klareis* (clear ice) forms at 0 to −3 °C [DWD]. Fog-frost deposits "show their typical growth against the wind," mostly on near-vertical surfaces, and can grow into heavy loads [DWD]. Deposits on tree branches often fall to the ground below [DWD-T].
- **Friedrich on snow.** He called snow "the great white cloth, the epitome of the highest purity, under which nature prepares for a new life" (cited from his letters in a museum text) [CDF-EICH].

## 5. How Friedrich studied and used trees

### 5.1 How much, and which trees

- Of about 1300 drawings and studies, about 400 have trees at the center or use them for expression. The arborist Roloff went through all of them for the Dresden museums [ROL]. Friedrich began tree studies in 1797, and they became very detailed from 1804. Oaks and spruces dominate, and he "hardly" drew limes [ROL]. In pine, spruce and fir studies he drew "twig by twig, in part even needle by needle" [ROL].
- The Berlin museum: "Friedrich gave no tree as much attention as the oak." He drew particular characterful trees precisely from nature and then used them several times in different pictures. Most stand around Gothic ruins, graveyards or dolmens, and it is often late autumn or winter. The trees are marked by storms or lightning, and their age shows in dead branches [CDF-EICH].
- Grummt assigns 404 of 1014 attributed sheets to 17 sketchbooks [KH p.47].

### 5.2 How he drew trees outdoors

- **Kit and habits.** He carried pencil, paper and eraser [KH p.47]. He wrote "in der Ferne" (in the distance) beside each trunk of two distant pines, drawn "by small strokes and hooks in a style familiar from many later drawings" [KH p.47]. On 20 April 1799 he traced "the intricate ramifications of the branches" of a leafless tree on a slope "down to the smallest detail." The shaded, branchless side of the trunk is given only by its "sinuous outline" [KH p.48]. A 1797 oak "after nature" has foliage "outlined in jagged lines" and coarse hatching [KH p.48]. A soft-pencil 1806 oak is built of parallel hatching with almost no modeling of volume [CDF-STORCH].
- **Viewpoint recorded.** He marked the horizon line "even in studies of tangled roots" and even on the lower part of a tree trunk. That means he drew sitting on the ground, and "whenever he translated a drawing into a painting, he consistently retained the perspective and spatial relationships recorded in the drawing" [BUSCH-V pp.77–78]. Without a horizon line he wrote "unten" or "von unten" (from below) [BUSCH-V p.78]. He also noted time of day and the sun's position [BUSCH-V p.78]. Busch links this to Valenciennes (German edition 1803): foliage below the horizon shows its top, foliage above it shows its underside [BUSCH-V p.78]. Valenciennes also advised noticing "all the little things about the bark, the moss, the roots, the sweep of the branches" [KÖR p.285].
- **Reworking.** He reworked pencil studies, mostly in the studio, with pen or brush in carbon or iron-gall ink and brown washes [KH p.48]. He kept to pencil outdoors all his life, with written color notes; only three sky oil sketches of his survive [CDF-ABEND].

### 5.3 Studies reused in paintings (dates from text sources)

| Study | Used in | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Oak, c.1804 (Karlsruhe sketchbook) | Left oak of *Dolmen in the Snow* (1807) | [WP-HÜN] |
| Oak, 1804; oak, 5 May 1809 | First oak right and second oak left of the ruin, *Abbey in the Oakwood* (1809–10). Most of its oaks come from studies made at Neubrandenburg in 1809 | [WP-ABT] |
| *Old Oak with Stork's Nest*, 23 May 1806 | Left oak of the sepia *Dolmen by the Sea* (1807); central oak of *The Solitary Tree* (1822), 15 years later | [CDF-STORCH; WP-EIN] |
| Study of vine leaves and beeches, 13/14 June 1809; *Group of Large Oaks*, 16 June 1809; tree studies, 9/12 June 1809 | Single oak left (with added twigs), group of four and two oaks right, *The Solitary Tree* | [WP-EIN] |
| *Two Tree Studies*, Neubrandenburg, 25/26 April 1809 ("Eiche") | Two oaks among stumps in *Winter Landscape* (Schwerin, 1811). The large oak in all three *Two Men/Man and Woman Contemplating the Moon* (hollowed crooked trunk from the lower study, zigzag branch from the upper, partly leafy study). *Ruins in Twilight* (1831) and *Forest, Late Autumn* (c.1835): "over a period of more than twenty years" | [MET PDF p.37] |
| Bare oak, 3 May 1809 | *The Tree of Crows* (c.1822): branches added at left and others lengthened to stretch across the picture | [WP-CROW; MET PDF p.16] |
| Detailed pencil study | Central tree group of *Winter Landscape* (London, 1811) | [NG p.49] |
| Spruces drawn 1807; tallest tree drawn 1804 | *The Cross in the Mountains*: when painting it in oil he replaced most trees of the sepia. The revised spruces are slimmer; only the 1804 tree kept its place | [BIRK p.238] |
| Tree study, 23 October 1801 (Oslo) | Leftmost tree of a late transparency, reused "after more than thirty years" | [MET PDF p.45] |

The Solitary Tree's oak is described as a composite of studies made between 1806 and 1810 [CDF-EIN; MET PDF p.40]. The bare oak in winter recurs in *Dolmen in the Snow* (1807), *Winter* (1808, burned 1931), *Abbey in the Oakwood*, *Monastery Graveyard in the Snow* (1819, lost) and *Oak in the Snow* (Cologne, 1827). *Oak Tree in Snow* (Berlin, 1829) is the most concentrated version [CDF-EICH]. For *Abbey* he wrote in 1809: "the oaks stretch their arms upward out of the fog, while below they have already quite vanished" [WP-ABT, quoting the letters].

### 5.4 Which paintings have which trees (from text)

- **Oaks.** *Dolmen in the Snow* (1807): three leafless oaks; the two upright ones have broken-out crowns, and the third has been bent by wind [WP-HÜN]. *Abbey in the Oakwood*: leafless oaks "with lopped branches," four on each side of the ruin [WP-ABT]. *Winter Landscape* (Schwerin, 1811): the "twisted trunks of two dead oak trees" and rows of stumps. Its London pendant sets "erect forms of the young fir trees" against "the tangled, disordered limbs of the dead oaks" [NG p.44]. *The Solitary Tree* (1822): a great oak whose top branches are dead [CDF-EIN]. *Two Men Contemplating the Moon* (Dresden, 1819): an uprooted, moss-covered oak held by a boulder, a spruce, a cut stump and a dead branch on the ground [WP-ZM]. In the Berlin variant the oak has "a much denser network of branches, and writhing, moss-covered roots." In the New York variant some green leaves remain on the oak [MET PDF pp.17, 19–20, 34]. *Oak Tree in Snow* (1829): an old oak, crownless and probably dead at the top, with gnarled, bent branches and "filigree twigs," and remains of a fallen trunk before it [CDF-EICH].
- **Spruce and fir.** *The Chasseur in the Forest* (c.1813): spruces with red-brown trunks, groups of young firs dusted with snow and two sawn stumps [CDF-CHASS]. *Early Snow* (1828): firs lining a path, a wall of spruces and one gently snow-covered spruce on the center line [CDF-FRÜH]. *Spruce Thicket in the Snow* (Munich) is the pendant of the Dresden *Trees and Bushes in the Snow* [CDF-GEB].
- **Bushes.** A reviewer of *Trees and Bushes in the Snow* (1828) wrote of "a group of shrubbery that crosses and intertwines leaflessly, rendered with the utmost truth to nature" [CDF-GEB].
- **Birch.** A late moonlit transparency shows moonlight on "the white trunk of the birch tree," the other trees making "dark filigree" [MET PDF p.44].
- **Willow.** See §5.6.
- **Beech, lime, alder.** A beech study fed *The Solitary Tree* [WP-EIN]. Lime studies of April–May 1808 survive [SKD-W], but Roloff says he hardly drew limes [ROL]. For alder I found no text naming it in any painting or study; evidence either way is missing.

### 5.5 How he painted them, according to conservators and scholars

- **Underdrawing includes the trees.** In the London *Winter Landscape* "an underdrawing for the rocks and trees is also visible." The painted layers "obey the outlines of the underdrawing," with pentimenti only "at the left and right-hand edge of the largest fir tree" [NG p.49]. In the unfinished *Entrance to a Graveyard*, infrared shows "the fluid drawing of foliage" in pen. He apparently drew the whole composition in pencil and then went over all of it in ink, "including fine details such as the grass and delicate leaf structure" [NG p.58].
- **Order.** In *Forest Interior by Moonlight* (1823/30), XRF maps show "the paint of the trees was applied on the already painted sky" [ALF p.346].
- **Strokes.** The firs of the London picture "are thinly painted with short, hatched strokes" [NG p.50]. In the New York *Two Men Contemplating the Moon* the forms are "less detailed … rendered with a fluid, assured brush" that needed no underdrawing [MET PDF pp.19–20].
- **Brushwork of bare twigs.** I found no technical text that describes how he painted fine bare twigs, such as brush type, stroke direction or wet versus dry paint. This is a gap.
- **Damage as he drew it.** Roloff notes that from 1806/10 on, his old oaks often have dead tops. Many limbs up to 25 m high look "sawn off" with smooth cuts, some 30–40 cm thick. That was hardly possible with the saws and climbing of the time, and no other Romantic painter shows so many "mutilated" trees. He reads it as artistic invention, not as a record of forestry [ROL]. The Berlin museum reads the dead branches as signs of great age [CDF-EICH].
- **Contemporary standard.** Carus, his friend, faulted painters who cannot see "the differences of outline between different species of trees" [CAR p.124]. He also faulted those who "confound all the specific forms of tree growth in an imaginary substance that they call 'foliage'" [CAR p.137].

### 5.6 Did he paint pollard willows?

**Yes, in at least one painting that the sources name, and he studied willows repeatedly. The motif is rare in his work.**

- *The Hut in the Snow* (*Verschneite Hütte*, 1827, 31 × 25 cm, Berlin). The museum text says the young shoots of "the willows behind" it are "vigorous" (*kräftigen jungen Trieben*) and herald spring [CDF-HÜT]. German Wikipedia, citing Hannesen 1985, calls them *Korbweiden* (basket willows) [WP-HÜT]. Clinger's UCL thesis names "pollard willows" in the picture and describes "the last season's willow growth scrambling upwards, their rise silhouetted against the murky winter's sky" [UCL p.26].
- Clinger also finds "pollard willows" on a floodplain, inclined diagonally, in a small *Winterlandschaft* (1827, 21 × 30 cm, private collection, Zittau). Its central trees are "nearly identical to those behind the Hut in the Snow" [UCL pp.56, 59]. That is a single scholar's identification.
- *Willow Bush under a Low Sun* (c.1832/35, Frankfurt): two willows "with burst trunks" grow from a thicket of twigs and undergrowth, with few leaves left [FDH-MD]. The catalog does not call them pollards.
- **Willow studies:** *Stump of a Willow with New Shoots*, 12 August 1799, pen and pencil (Berlin) [CDF-STUMPF]. A willow noted "ganz grau" (quite gray), 21 April 1808 (Dresden) [SKD-W]. *Study of a Willow, Study of Two Branches*, 18 April/2 June 1809 (Berlin) [CDF-WEIDE; KH caption]. *Willow Struck by Lightning*, 19 March 1812 (Prague) [BUSCH-V fig.3]. A willow stands behind a figure group in a 1799 design [CDF-KRIEB]. Whether the 1799 "stump with new shoots" is a lopped pollard is not stated. The title fits one, but that is my reading.
- **Against frequency:** Roloff, who went through all his drawings, writes that lopping (*Schneitelung*) and limbing of the lower trunk were occasionally practiced then, but "there are almost no pictures of it by CDF," though more by other painters [ROL].

## Gaps

- No source gives the number of rods on a willow pollard head or measured rod angles. The same goes for per-species branching angles and the number of branch orders.
- Pfister and Schneebeli (1999) on snow and board width was read only through secondary summaries [PS99].
- No technical study describes Friedrich's brushwork for bare twigs. Grummt's catalogue raisonné (2011), which would list every willow and tree study, was not accessible; I relied on museum records and the SKD 2024 catalog excerpt.
- The *Winterlandschaft* (1827, Zittau) pollards rest on one thesis.
